newsitem.title: USA: DLR/MARK SLUMPS AT US NOON, STERLING WOES PERSIST.
newsitem.headline: DLR/MARK SLUMPS AT US NOON, STERLING WOES PERSIST.

text.p: The dollar was weaker at midday, slumping to session lows against the mark in sympathy with a battered British pound, which fell sharply in Europe after the Bank of England signalled that Thursday's rate hike could be the last for some time.

Sterling dropped to a 10-month trough of $1.5780 and crumbled to a low of 2.9640 marks in European dealings following the central bank's announcement that it had raised official interest rates by 25 basis points to 7.0 percent.
Dealers had focussed on the policy committee's post-meeting statement, which suggested that interest rates had now reached a level consistent with the Bank of England's inflation target.

At midday, the pound was still lingering below 2.97 marks and remained capped below $1.59. The dollar had slumped below 1.87 marks to trade near session lows at 1.8685/95 versus an opening rate of 1.8755/60.
"We're in mop up mode here in New York," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.

Analysts said the Bank of England's statement had sent sterling/mark through key neckline support of a head-and-shoulders formation pattern at 2.9880, accelerating the losses and spilling over into dollar/mark.
Dollar/mark's slide flushed out shaky long positions and set off stop-loss selling below 1.87 just before midday. But dealers predicted little long-term damage.
"It's clear that the interbank market got ahead of itself in looking for a continued rise in dollar/mark," said Jeremy Fand, foreign exchange strategist at Bank of Boston.

"But this retracement should provide the opportunity for longer-term players, mainly the fund management community, to get on board," he said. "Although they're late to the party, they still need to buy dollars."
The dollar was confined to a much more narrow range against the yen, holding above the 118 threshold for much of the U.S. morning.
A recovery in mark/yen, which slid to a two-year low of 62.73 in Asian trade, helped support dollar/yen, dealers said.

But caution reigned ahead Japanese current account data for June, due on Friday. Economists' forecasts for Japan's surplus ranged from 840 billion yen to 1.1 trillion yen -- a reflection of recent volatility in the numbers.

Stern warnings from U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky in recent days have heightened the anxiety level of dollar/yen bulls. Barshefsky has repeatedly warned Japan not to export its way out of its current economic malaise.
"The trade issue has been on the back burner for a while, but Barshefsky's comments have helped move it back to the forefront," said Fand.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television on Thursday, Jerry Jasinowski, the president of the National Association of Manufacturers, said the dollar was "a bit too high" and predicted that it would come down from its current levels in 1998.
At midday, the dollar was changing hands at 118.30/40 yen, just below its opening rate of 118.39/44.
Elsewhere, sterling was weaker at $1.5870/80 against $1.5885/95. Despite its losses against the mark, the dollar was stronger at 1.5297/07 Swiss francs against 1.5275/85.
It was little changed at Canadian $1.3870/75 versus C$1.3871/76 at the open.
